[2023 summer phd probability — problem 5]

Part II, Exercise. Let $U$ be valued on $\{1, 2, 3\}$ with pmf $P(U=1) = \tfrac12$, $P(U=2) = \tfrac13$, $P(U=3) = \tfrac16$.
(a) Construct a coupling $(X, Y)$ — give its pmf as a $3 \times 3$ table — such that $X \stackrel{d}{=} U$; $Y$ has $P(Y=1) = 0$ and $P(Y=k) = P(U=k \mid U \ge 2)$ for $k = 2, 3$; $P(X \le Y) = 1$ and $P(Y \le X + 1) = 1$.
(b) Prove or disprove that this coupling is optimal (i.e. the TV distance between the marginals equals $P(X \ne Y)$).

response.text:
### (a) Construction of the coupling

The marginal distribution of \(Y\) is

\[
P(Y=1)=0,\qquad 
P(Y=2)=P(U=2\mid U\ge 2)=\frac{1/3}{1/3+1/6}=\frac23,
\]

and

\[
P(Y=3)=P(U=3\mid U\ge 2)=\frac{1/6}{1/3+1/6}=\frac13.
\]

We need \(X\stackrel d=U\), so

\[
P(X=1)=\frac12,\qquad P(X=2)=\frac13,\qquad P(X=3)=\frac16.
\]

The constraints

\[
P(X\le Y)=1,\qquad P(Y\le X+1)=1
\]

force the support of \((X,Y)\) to lie in the set

\[
\{(1,2),(2,2),(2,3),(3,3)\},
\]

since \(Y=1\) has probability \(0\).

Let the joint pmf be written as a \(3\times 3\) table with rows indexed by \(X\) and columns indexed by \(Y\). A valid coupling is

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc|c}
 & Y=1 & Y=2 & Y=3 & P_X \\ \hline
X=1 & 0 & \frac12 & 0 & \frac12 \\
X=2 & 0 & \frac16 & \frac16 & \frac13 \\
X=3 & 0 & 0 & \frac16 & \frac16 \\ \hline
P_Y & 0 & \frac23 & \frac13 & 1
\end{array}
\]

Indeed, the row sums are

\[
\left(\frac12,\frac13,\frac16\right),
\]

so \(X\stackrel d=U\), and the column sums are

\[
\left(0,\frac23,\frac13\right),
\]

so \(Y\) has the desired distribution. Also, every nonzero entry satisfies

\[
X\le Y\le X+1,
\]

so

\[
P(X\le Y)=1,\qquad P(Y\le X+1)=1.
\]

---

### (b) Optimality

For two probability measures \(\mu,\nu\) on a countable space, their total variation distance is

\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\nu)
=
\frac12\sum_x |\mu(x)-\nu(x)|.
\]

Here

\[
\mu=\mathcal L(X)=\left(\frac12,\frac13,\frac16\right),
\qquad
\nu=\mathcal L(Y)=\left(0,\frac23,\frac13\right).
\]

Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\nu)
&=
\frac12\left(
\left|\frac12-0\right|
+
\left|\frac13-\frac23\right|
+
\left|\frac16-\frac13\right|
\right) \\
&=
\frac12\left(
\frac12+\frac13+\frac16
\right) \\
&=
\frac12.
\end{aligned}
\]

On the other hand, for the coupling constructed in part (a),

\[
P(X=Y)=P(X=2,Y=2)+P(X=3,Y=3)
=
\frac16+\frac16
=
\frac13.
\]

Hence

\[
P(X\neq Y)=1-P(X=Y)=1-\frac13=\frac23.
\]

Thus

\[
P(X\neq Y)=\frac23
\neq
\frac12
=
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal L(X),\mathcal L(Y)).
\]

Therefore this coupling is **not optimal** in the total variation sense. An optimal, or maximal, coupling would satisfy

\[
P(X\neq Y)=d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal L(X),\mathcal L(Y)).
\]

So the coupling from part (a) is not optimal.
